analysis.one_liner: Extends the lower tax rates on capital gains and dividends through 2010, paired with a one-year increase in the alternative minimum tax exemption.
analysis.headline: Congress passed it and President Bush signed it on May 17, 2006, extending the reduced capital gains and dividend tax rates through 2010 by votes of 244-185 in the House and 54-44 in the Senate — after dropping the Senate's two-year AMT fix, tuition deduction, veterans' health funding, and larger oil-company tax increases.
analysis.plain_summary: This law extends the reduced 15% tax rates on capital gains and dividend income through 2010, extends richer small-business expensing allowances through 2009, and raises the alternative minimum tax exemption for 2006 only. To pay for it, it raises some estimated-tax payments from large corporations, requires faster amortization of drilling exploration costs for the biggest oil companies, extends the 'kiddie tax' to children under 18, and requires 3% withholding on government payments to contractors. In the Senate, Democrats had added two years of AMT relief, an extension of the tuition deduction, $1 billion for veterans' health facilities, and bigger oil-company tax increases — all of which were stripped in the House-Senate conference.
analysis.who_benefits: Investors who pay taxes on capital gains and dividends — a benefit that concentrates heavily among high-income households, since that is where capital gains and dividends are earned — plus large financial companies whose overseas active-financing income stays exempt, and small businesses that can keep expensing up to $100,000 of equipment through 2009.

how_it_helps.text: Extends through 2010 the reduced tax rates on capital gains and dividend income that were otherwise scheduled to expire after 2008.

Raises the alternative minimum tax exemption for 2006 to $62,550 for singles and $42,500 for couples and lets personal credits offset AMT liability for that year, protecting millions of households from a tax originally aimed at the very wealthy.
Extends through 2009 the ability of small businesses to immediately expense up to $100,000 of equipment rather than depreciating it over years.
Extends through 2008 the exemption of foreign banks', finance, and insurance income of controlled foreign corporations from Subpart F taxation.

analysis.who_pays: The Treasury (and future taxpayers) bear the cost of the rate extension; the gap is filled with offsets: higher estimated-tax payments from corporations with $1 billion or more in assets, a five-year instead of two-year amortization of geological and geophysical expenditures for major integrated oil companies, the kiddie tax extended to children under 18, tighter rules on taxpayers negotiating offers-in-compromise with the IRS, and a 3% withholding requirement on government payments to contractors starting after 2010.
analysis.who_pays_short: The Treasury; large corporations and oil majors

drawbacks.text: The AMT relief lasts only one year: the higher exemption applies to 2006 only, so the same exposure returns the following year and Congress has to patch it repeatedly.

The conference report drops the Senate-passed two-year AMT exemption extension, the tuition and fees deduction extension, and the $1 billion Veterans Hospital Improvement Fund, along with the Senate's repeal of preferential treatment of major oil companies' LIFO inventories and their foreign tax credit claims.

The remaining oil-company offset is narrow — five-year amortization of geological and geophysical expenditures for the largest producers — while the Senate's larger revenue raisers (LIFO revaluation and foreign tax credit denial, projected at billions) were rejected in conference.

The bill leans on timing shifts rather than real revenue: it makes corporations with $1 billion or more in assets pay 105% of their September 2006 estimated tax and boosts 2012-2013 payments while delaying 2010-2011 payments, which meets budget-window rules by moving money between years.

The 3% withholding on government payments to vendors, set to start in 2011, was widely criticized by contractors and governments as an administrative burden (and was later repealed by a later Congress).

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit flows to investors whose capital gains and dividends are taxed at 15%, which is where the largest dollar gains sit, and the offsetting AMT patch protects middle- and upper-middle-income families for only a single year. The Senate had crafted a version with a two-year AMT fix, a tuition deduction extension, veterans' health money, and bigger oil-company offsets, and every attempt to steer the conference toward those priorities was voted down along party lines. What emerged is a bill whose centerpiece is a multi-year extension of rates concentrated at the top, paid for partly by accounting shifts.

outcome.mechanism: Both chambers passed it — the House 244-185 and the Senate 54-44 on the conference report — and President Bush signed it on May 17, 2006.

narrative.text: Introduced November 10, 2005 by Rep. Bill Thomas with no cosponsors, the House bill extended expiring tax provisions, including the capital gains and dividend rate cuts through 2010, and passed the House 234-197 on December 8, 2005.

The Senate added its own version with a two-year AMT exemption increase, an extended tuition deduction, a $1 billion veterans' hospital improvement fund, and oil-company revenue provisions, passing it 66-31 on February 2, 2006.

In conference instructions, the Senate voted 92-0 to direct conferees to keep the veterans' health funding, but motions to reject the capital gains and dividend extension (Dodd, 40-53; Kennedy, 47-53; Reed, 45-55) and to bar any deficit increase (Lautenberg, 46-54) all failed on near-party-line votes.

In the House, five separate motions to instruct conferees — from Neal, Tanner, Rangel, Cardin, McDermott, and Larson — to prioritize AMT relief, keep the tuition deduction, and drop the capital gains extension all failed by wide margins.

The final conference report kept the capital gains and dividend rate extension through 2010 and only one year of AMT relief, required five-year amortization of exploration costs for major integrated oil companies instead of the Senate's larger oil tax increases, and dropped the veterans' funding and tuition deduction.
The conference report passed the House 244-185 and the Senate 54-44, was signed by President Bush on May 17, 2006, and became Public Law 109-222.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-income investors gained a multi-year extension of the 15% capital gains and dividend rates, and the major oil companies avoided the Senate's larger tax increases, keeping only a narrower exploration-cost amortization requirement. Households facing the alternative minimum tax got relief, but only for one tax year.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High-income investors; oil companies avoided bigger tax hikes

for.name: Bill Thomas
for.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill, steered it through committee and the House floor, requested the conference, and brought up the conference report for final passage.

for.name: 229 of 231 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Voted for final passage of the House bill (225 of 231) and for the conference report (229 of 231), and against every Democratic motion to recommit or instruct conferees.

for.name: Charles Grassley
for.what_they_did: Managed the Senate floor consideration, served as a Senate conferee, and offered the instruction motion combining AMT hold-harmless relief with the capital gains and dividend extension, which passed 53-47.

for.name: 51 of 55 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Voted 51-3 to pass the Senate version and 51-3 to adopt the conference report, rejecting motions to instruct conferees on veterans' funding, military readiness, and oil-company tax provisions.

for.name: President George W. Bush
for.what_they_did: Signed the bill into law on May 17, 2006.

against.name: Charles Rangel
against.role: Ranking Member, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Offered a motion to recommit on the House floor and repeated motions to instruct conferees to expand AMT relief, drop the capital gains and dividend extension, and avoid increasing the deficit; all failed.

against.name: 182 of 201 House Democrats
against.what_they_did: Voted 193-9 against House passage, 182-15 against the conference report, and nearly unanimously for motions to recommit and instruct conferees.

against.name: 40 of 44 Senate Democrats
against.what_they_did: Voted 26-17 against the Senate version, 40-3 against the conference report, and nearly unanimously for instructions on veterans' funding, AMT hold-harmless, and oil-company tax provisions.

against.name: Christopher Dodd
against.what_they_did: Moved to instruct Senate conferees to keep the $1 billion veterans' health funding instead of extending capital gains and dividend tax breaks for people with incomes over $1 million; rejected 40-53.

against.name: Edward Kennedy
against.what_they_did: Moved to instruct Senate conferees to reject the extension of the capital gains and dividend rate reductions; rejected 47-53.

against.name: Barack Obama
against.what_they_did: Moved to instruct Senate conferees to provide tax relief for low-income Hurricane Katrina victims and poor families eligible for the child tax credit; the motion was withdrawn before a vote.

sides.party_line_note: Every key vote split heavily by party: House passage was 225 of 231 Republicans for versus 9 of 202 Democrats, the House conference report 229-2 versus 15-182, and the Senate conference report 51 of 55 Republicans for versus 3 of 44 Democrats.

industries.note: The bill's centerpiece extends the 15% capital gains and dividend rates through 2010; because most capital gains and dividends go to high-income households, most of the revenue forgone accrues to them, while the Treasury and future taxpayers bear the cost.

The final law requires the five largest producers to amortize exploration costs over five years instead of two, but the Senate's larger increases — LIFO inventory revaluation and denial of their foreign tax credits — were stripped in conference. The industry's central interest in the bill was defeating those offsets.

industries.industry: Banks, finance and insurance companies with foreign operations
industries.note: The bill extends through 2008 the exemption of active foreign banking, finance, and insurance income from Subpart F taxation, keeping that income out of U.S. tax.

Starting after 2010, governments must withhold 3% of payments for goods and services, improving tax collection but straining contractors' cash flow; the provision was later repealed by a subsequent Congress.

industries.industry: Families with wealthy parents and children with investment income
industries.note: The kiddie tax now applies to children under 18 rather than 14, taxing their passive income at the parents' rate — a revenue offset that falls on affluent families, while the Roth IRA conversion income limit repeal benefits savers at all income levels who want to convert.
